newsitem.title: USA: Rail rivals defend Conrail proposals to shippers.
newsitem.headline: Rail rivals defend Conrail proposals to shippers.

text.p: A day before a meeting of the top railroad executives involved in the battle for Conrail, each side claimed Thursday its merger proposal would offer better service to freight shippers.

Speaking to a gathering of coal shippers at the National Mining Association's annual transportation seminar here, executives from Richmond, Va.-based CSX Corp. and Conrail sought to reassure shippers that a merger of the two companies would not result in sharply higher freight rates.
"Conrail and CSX offer the greatest amount of synergy potential," said Conrail Senior Vice President Timothy Dwyer. "Our merger proposal is not about foreclosing inter-line competition."
Coal shipments between mines and utilities account for about 40 percent of all major rail freight transportation in the United States.
Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern Corp. maintained that its plan offered shippers a more balanced rail network.
Philadelphia-based Conrail and CSX have agreed on a cash-and-stock merger worth $9.5 billion, while rival bidder Norfolk Southern has offered $10.3 billion in cash, or $115 a share for Conrail.

The chief executives of the three railroads plan to hold the meeting in a major step aimed at resolving a stalemate in the takeover battle. Norfolk Southern Chief Executive Officer David Goode is to meet with Conrail Chief Executive David LeVan and CSX Chief Executive John Snow.
So far both sides have continued to defend their original proposals.

Dwyer said the advantages of a CSX-Conrail deal would become fully apparent in March, when the companies are slated to file their merger proposal to the Surface Transportation Board, the federal authority that oversees railroads.
Ray Sharp, vice president for coal and sales marketing at CSX Transportation, said the deal would be a "good news" story for both coal shippers and utilities.
"This merger creates a more unified rail system ... so that shippers will no longer have to depend on two or three railroads to get their freight moved," he said.
Meanwhile, Norfolk Southern asserted its offer was "superior in every way."

"A Norfolk Southern-Conrail combination would more evenly balance competition in almost any measure imaginable, but particularly on the coal side," said Bill Fox, vice president of coal marketing at Norfolk Southern.

Fox told the audience packed with coal shippers that a link-up of Norfolk Southern and Conrail would fairly evenly divide rail carriers' access to power plants in the eastern half of the country. By contrast, a CSX-Conrail merger would give the newly formed company exclusive access to three-fourths of the region's utilities, he said.
Shippers say they remained wary of any consolidation.
"We highly endorse competition," said Joseph Lema, vice president of the National Mining Association. "There is less of a threat of difficulties if the status quo remained."
